title: The Almanac, Revised
part: PART FOUR: HOLDING UP THE BRIDGE

pages.text:
*From the Bridgewater Almanac (revised): Look under the bridge. You may be surprised at who is holding it up.*

The bunting was indeed damp, and the singing was worse. A new plank sat in the middle of the old bridge, painted a cheerful yellow. It bore a name in Perrin’s careful, ink-stained hand. It was the first time Hobb’s name had been written down anywhere in Bridgewater, and the first time it had been read aloud.

He was the guest of honor, which meant he was standing very still and trying to look like a bridge rather than a person. For the first ten minutes, he hid behind Gran, who was holding a scone like a shield and looking very proud. Then the small children noticed him.

They did not climb him. They inspected him. One boy poked a mossy ear. A girl asked if he had a pocket for her marble. Hobb, who was ten feet tall and shy as a rabbit in a meadow, looked down at the sea of freckled faces. He found that he was smiling.

It was a terrifying, wonderful thing to be seen.
pages.image: A mossy, grey-green troll with round spectacles and a patched waistcoat stands on a stone bridge, surrounded by small children poking his ears and holding out marbles, while a woman in a blue ribbon hat stands protectively nearby.

pages.text:
The Bridge Club had dissolved into something quieter, something that smelled of flour and wood shavings. It was the Toll Table. Skye Tanner, Cedric Pettibone, and Perrin Fen ran it. The rules were simple: you paid a story, and you received a scone.

Cedric was very good at sweeping. He did not sweep the way he used to, with his back to the work and his eyes on the crowd. He swept the bridge, stone by stone, with a broom that was almost as tall as he was. He and Hobb were working out a complicated thing. Apologies, it turned out, could only fix the small breaks. The deep cracks required mornings. Many of them. Cedric swept. Hobb mended the railings. They did not always speak, but they did not look away.

Skye held the ledger. Perrin drew the stories as they were told, so they would not vanish into the air. It was a decent arrangement. It was, in fact, a good one.
pages.image: A skinny boy in a red waistcoat sweeps a stone bridge with a tall broom, while a tall girl with a long braid holds a ledger and a quiet boy in a wool hat sketches on a slate, a mossy troll watching from behind a railing.

pages.text:
Then the horn came. It was a long, steady blast that rolled up the river and shook the bunting in the trees. The *Persistent* was around the bend, her hull white against the brown water.

On the deck, Mari Alder stood with her blue cap on backwards, waving both arms. She was laughing, or she was shouting, and it was impossible to tell the difference from this distance. Rue, who had been standing on the bridge with a scone in each hand, dropped them. They hit the stone with a soft thud.

She ran. She ran faster than she had ever run in her life, her boots slapping the wet stone, her chest heaving with a thumping that felt like a trapped moth. Mari caught her in mid-air, and for a moment the world was just warm arms and the smell of river mud and joy. Over her mother’s shoulder, Rue saw Gran and Hobb, at either end of the bridge, both waving.
pages.image: A tall woman in a blue cap and sunburnt face stands on a barge deck waving with both arms, while a small girl in a mustard-yellow raincoat runs up a stone bridge toward her, with a mossy troll and an older woman waving from the bridge ends.

pages.text:
Mayor Ambrose Pettibone stood on his soapbox, wearing his top hat and holding the *Bridgewater Almanac*. The book was covered in red ink, with the old rules about hunger and wickedness crossed out in thick, angry lines. He had written new ones in his careful, looping hand, and now he read them aloud.

His voice was small. "Look under the bridge. You may be surprised at who is holding it up."

He paused, and the square went very quiet. The Mayor looked at Hobb, who was doing his best to look like a tree, but was mostly succeeding as a very large, mossy bush. Then the Mayor sat down on his soapbox, which let out a loud, wooden creak that echoed off the stone walls.

"I should like to add," he said, to the sudden cheering that followed, "that I was mistaken about a great many things."

It was the best speech he had ever given, and he did not do it again.
pages.image: A round man in a top hat and chain of office sits on a wooden soapbox, looking sheepish, while a mossy troll with round spectacles stands nearby holding a broom, and a crowd of townspeople applauds in a sunny square.

pages.text:
Dusk settled over the river, thick and blue. Rue and Hobb sat on the stone parapet, their feet hanging over the water. Biscuit, the enormous orange cat, slept in Hobb’s lap, his tail twitching with every rumble of a purr. Perrin sat between them, his pencil moving quickly as he traced the curve of the arch.

Rue told him the last story. It was about a girl who believed that being useful was a cure for loneliness. She described the cold bench by the school wall and the squashed cheese sandwich she had eaten in careful, small bites. She told him about the feeling of her heart, heavy and cold, sitting at the bottom of her pocket like a wet stone. She admitted she had been wrong.

Hobb listened. He did not apologize, and he did not tell her it would pass. He simply rested his broad, warm palm on the top of her head.

"Somebody has to hold it up," he said, his voice low and steady.

"Right then," Rue whispered. She leaned her head against his shoulder, which was as wide and solid as the bridge itself.
pages.image: A small girl with curly red-brown hair in two puffs leans her head against the shoulder of a large, mossy troll with round spectacles, both sitting on a stone bridge parapet at dusk, with an orange cat sleeping in the troll's lap.
